source: Mohammadirad, Masoud & Shuan Osman Karim. 2025. The development of imperfective and subjunctive marking in Hewramî. Linguistics 63(5): 1265–1292.
claim: The article reconstructs how regular phonological change conditioned the loss and redistribution of imperfective/subjunctive prefixes across Hewramî and neighboring Goranî varieties, using comparative dialect evidence and multi-generational recordings.
lect_scope: core Hewramî plus comparative Goranî varieties including Text, Luhon, Bizłane, Qela/Zerdeyane and others
time_scope: diachronic reconstruction plus contemporary generational variation

claim: A relevant regular sound change reduces pretonic /e/ to /i/ before a stressed syllable; the authors identify this as a widespread regional development also affecting Southern Kurdish and Laki.

The reduced vowel /i/ is subsequently lost in most contexts, except where deletion would violate syllable structure; the analysis explicitly relates this to synchronically epenthetic i/u used to repair illegal clusters.
After loss of the reduced vowel, initial mC clusters undergo reduction to C, removing the segmental reflex of the imperfective prefix in the relevant forms.

The comparative pattern preserves successive stages: me- in many Goranî varieties; mi- after pretonic reduction in Qela/Zerdeyane; m- after vowel loss; and Ø- after cluster reduction in core Hewramî, with stress becoming the surviving exponent in some cells.

In Text and Luhon the historical prefixes may be segmentally absent while stress placement remains as the grammatical reflex distinguishing TAM categories, illustrating morphologization of a prosodic residue after segmental erosion.
Loss of TAM/imperfective prefixes through phonological change is presented as a wider Iranic-and-neighboring tendency, not an isolated Hewramî development.

Multi-generational recordings show ongoing prefix loss: a younger Text speaker explicitly contrasts the father's biřeme 'run!' with the younger form řeme; the authors describe verb-class switching as gradual and cell-by-cell.

Because i [ɪ] and u [ʊ] are also used synchronically to break up illegal clusters, the authors caution that deciding whether individual i/u tokens are underlying vowels or epenthetic zero-reflexes is analytically nontrivial.
